newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters president hails deal with UPS.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters president hails deal with UPS.

text.p: United Parcel Service, the world's largest parcel delivery company, has reached a tentative agreement to end a 15-day Teamsters strike that crippled the delivery of packages nationwide, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman said early on Tuesday.
"I am pleased to announce that the United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union have reached a tentative settlement," she told a news conference shortly after midnight.
The strike by 185,000 Teamsters had crippled the world's largest carrier of small packages, costing UPS $650 million in lost business.
Ron Carey, president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said 10,000 new full-time jobs would be created over the five-year life of the tentative contract.

"We won in this agreement 10,000 new full-time jobs by combining existing low-wage, part-time positions," Carey said, adding that figure was in addition to jobs created by company growth or attrition. Before the strike, the company had committed to creating only 1,000 new full-time jobs for part-timers.
Carey said the union turned back the company's demand to pull out of the Teamsters multi-employer pension plans and start a new company-controlled pension plan.
In addition, he said the union had won very large pension increases for its members, the same or better than the company had offered before the strike.

He said the new contract also contained substantial wage increases, including for part-timers who make up about 60 percent of all employees, to $15 an hour by the end of the five-year contract from the current $11 an hour.
"This strike marks a new era," Carey said. "American workers have shown that if we stand up to corporate greed, this victory shows that american workers are on the move again."
"This is not just a Teamster victory, this is a victory for all working people," Carey said at a news conference at Teamster headquarters.
Carey said workers may start returning to work as early as Wednesday night, even though a formal ratification vote will take longer.
President Bill Clinton patted both sides on the back in an early-morning statement read to reporters in Edgartown, Massachusetts, where he was on vacation.

"Today's agreement represents their hard work and determination to reconcile their differences for the good of the company, its employees and the customers they serve," Clinton said. "The issues that were at the heart of their negotiations are important to our nation's economic strength, and to all Americans."

Carey said he expected the company to carry out at least some temporary layoffs while its business begins to return to normal. Before the strike began Aug. 4, UPS handled 12 million items on a normal weekday.
The chief UPS negotiator, Dave Murray, joined Carey in paying tribute to Herman, the labor secretary, for having nursed the contract talks to a successful conclusion.
Murray said the company wanted to address its employs before speaking publicly.
Herman said the the company and the union together created "a model workplace" for the 21st century.
The two sides began their latest round of talks on Thursday at the request of Herman. The talks continued for more than 80 hours, except for brief sleep breaks.
The strike involved more workers than any other walkout in over a decade.
